scenes.visual: THE WORLD for both films (16:9, dark navy background, flat cartoon style, no molecular structures). Colour map, fixed: BACTERIA are BLUE, ARCHAEA (including methanogens) are ORANGE, EUKARYOTES (yeast, fungi, protists, animals, plants) are GREEN. Ribosomal RNA strands are drawn as a WHITE ribbon of small beads. Similarity scores are white numbers in grid cells; any tree or grid not computed from real data carries a small corner label 'schematic'. Title card 'Look Alike, Far Apart' fades in over two small capsule-shaped cells side by side, one BLUE, one ORANGE, both drifting slightly.

scenes.tts: A methanogen and E. coli look almost the same under a microscope. Are they close relatives? Both are small cells with no nucleus. A methanogen makes methane, and this one lives in a cow's rumen.
scenes.caption: A methanogen and E. coli look almost the same under a microscope. Are they close relatives? Both are small cells with no nucleus. A methanogen makes methane, and this one lives in a cow's rumen.
scenes.visual: A round microscope field. Two grey, identical-looking capsule cells sit side by side, labelled 'methanogen' and 'E. coli'. A dashed outline where a nucleus would be appears inside each, then fades, with the label 'no nucleus'. A small cartoon cow appears top-left with an arrow to the methanogen: 'from a cow's rumen'. A white question mark pulses between the two cells.
scenes.narration: A methanogen and E. coli look almost the same under a microscope. Are they close relatives? Both are small cells with no nucleus. A methanogen makes methane, and this one lives in a cow's rumen.

scenes.tts: For a long time, biologists lumped all cells without a nucleus together as prokaryotes. But that grouping rests on something missing. Two cells can both lack a nucleus and still be distant relatives.
scenes.visual: Both grey cells slide into one box labelled 'prokaryotes: no nucleus'. The word 'no' glows red. The box's floor cracks down the middle, and a gap opens between the two cells, labelled 'related?'
scenes.narration: For a long time, biologists lumped all cells without a nucleus together as prokaryotes. But that grouping rests on something missing. Two cells can both lack a nucleus and still be distant relatives.

scenes.tts: Carl Woese looked for a part that every cell carries, doing the same job in each. He chose the ribosome, the particle that makes proteins. Inside its small subunit lies a strand of R N A.
scenes.caption: Carl Woese looked for a part that every cell carries, doing the same job in each. He chose the ribosome, the particle that makes proteins. Inside its small subunit lies a strand of RNA.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one cell. A ribosome drawn as two rounded blobs, large and small, labelled 'ribosome'. The small blob is labelled 'small subunit'; a white bead ribbon unspools out of it, labelled 'small-subunit ribosomal RNA'. A name card 'Carl Woese' sits in the lower corner.
scenes.narration: Carl Woese looked for a part that every cell carries, doing the same job in each. He chose the ribosome, the particle that makes proteins. Inside its small subunit lies a strand of RNA.

scenes.tts: His laboratory pulled this small-subunit ribosomal R N A from many microbes. They cut each strand into pieces and compared the pieces, organism by organism. Each pair got a similarity score.
scenes.caption: His laboratory pulled this small-subunit ribosomal RNA from many microbes. They cut each strand into pieces and compared the pieces, organism by organism. Each pair got a similarity score.
scenes.visual: Five white bead ribbons line up in rows, each tagged with a small coloured cell icon: two ORANGE methanogens, BLUE E. coli, BLUE Bacillus, GREEN yeast. Scissors snip each ribbon into short segments. Matching segments between two rows light up yellow, and a counter beside the pair ticks upward.
scenes.narration: His laboratory pulled this small-subunit ribosomal RNA from many microbes. They cut each strand into pieces and compared the pieces, organism by organism. Each pair got a similarity score.

scenes.tts: Here is the logic. Small changes pile up in the R N A as lineages separate. So fewer differences usually mean a more recent common ancestor.
scenes.caption: Here is the logic. Small changes pile up in the RNA as lineages separate. So fewer differences usually mean a more recent common ancestor.
scenes.visual: One ribbon splits into two branches that grow rightward over time. Red dots (changes) appear one by one along each branch, a little faster on one branch than the other. A slider labelled 'time since common ancestor' moves right and the red dots multiply. On-screen rule: 'fewer differences: usually a more recent common ancestor'.
scenes.narration: Here is the logic. Small changes pile up in the RNA as lineages separate. So fewer differences usually mean a more recent common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Now the scores fill a grid, one cell for every pair. A stated grouping method can then propose a tree from the grid. Different methods make different assumptions, so the grid alone does not fix one tree.
scenes.visual: A 5 x 5 grid fills with qualitative cells (darker = more shared pieces), rows and columns tagged with the five coloured icons; corner label 'schematic'. Beside the grid, a tree is drawn, label 'proposed by a grouping method'; the two methanogen tips sit together and the two bacteria together. No root is marked. A small tag under the tree: 'other methods, other assumptions'. The grid stays on screen next to the tree.
scenes.narration: Now the scores fill a grid, one cell for every pair. A stated grouping method can then propose a tree from the grid. Different methods make different assumptions, so the grid alone does not fix one tree.

scenes.tts: Methanogens look like bacteria. So where do you think they landed on the tree? Close to E. coli, or somewhere else?
scenes.visual: The tree with the BLUE bacteria and GREEN yeast tips placed; the two methanogen tips float above it, ORANGE, with two dotted arrows: one toward the blue branch, one hovering. Text on screen: 'Where do the methanogens land?'
scenes.narration: Methanogens look like bacteria. So where do you think they landed on the tree? Close to E. coli, or somewhere else?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame. A small pause icon and a countdown ring in the corner.

scenes.tts: Not among the bacteria. Woese and George Fox reported that methanogens formed their own group. It sat about as far from bacteria as from eukaryotes, the cells with a nucleus.
scenes.visual: The methanogen tips drop onto a third, ORANGE branch of their own. Three branches now: BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN. Brackets show the ORANGE-to-BLUE distance and the ORANGE-to-GREEN distance as about equal. Label '1977: Woese and Fox'.
scenes.narration: Not among the bacteria. Woese and George Fox reported that methanogens formed their own group. It sat about as far from bacteria as from eukaryotes, the cells with a nucleus.

scenes.tts: They first called the new group archaebacteria. Later, Woese and colleagues proposed three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Those names are still the standard labels.
scenes.visual: Branch labels write themselves: BLUE 'Bacteria', ORANGE 'Archaea', GREEN 'Eukarya'. A small date tag '1990' slides in. The old label 'archaebacteria' fades out above the orange branch.
scenes.narration: They first called the new group archaebacteria. Later, Woese and colleagues proposed three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Those names are still the standard labels.

scenes.tts: What do the scores tell us, and what don't they? They rank closeness. They do not date a split, and they do not reveal an ancestor.
scenes.visual: Two stamps over the tree: a green check beside 'ranks closeness', red crosses beside 'dates a split' and 'shows an ancestor'. The tree stays visible underneath.
scenes.narration: What do the scores tell us, and what don't they? They rank closeness. They do not date a split, and they do not reveal an ancestor.

scenes.tts: Across the deepest splits, repeated changes at one site can blur the signal in a single molecule. Many genes and better models of change sharpen the branching pattern. But which branch came off first also needs an outside reference.
scenes.visual: Zoom to the base of the tree, where the three branches meet close together; the branching blurs and wobbles, with red dots stacking on the same bead to show repeated changes. Many coloured ribbons (labelled 'many genes + models of change') stream in and the branching pattern sharpens, but no root is marked. A tag appears at the base: 'which came first? needs an outside reference'.
scenes.narration: Across the deepest splits, repeated changes at one site can blur the signal in a single molecule. Many genes and better models of change sharpen the branching pattern. But which branch came off first also needs an outside reference.

scenes.tts: Most recent trees of this kind place eukaryotes inside the archaea, closest to a group called the Asgard archaea. Exactly where is still debated. On that view, life has two primary branches, Bacteria and Archaea.
scenes.visual: The tree redraws, labelled 'schematic': two primary branches, BLUE 'Bacteria' and ORANGE 'Archaea'. Inside the orange branch, a bracketed cluster of several orange twigs is labelled 'Asgard archaea'. The GREEN 'Eukarya' branch grows out from among or beside that cluster, its base drawn as a soft blur. A small tag: 'exact position debated'.
scenes.narration: Most recent trees of this kind place eukaryotes inside the archaea, closest to a group called the Asgard archaea. Exactly where is still debated. On that view, life has two primary branches, Bacteria and Archaea.

scenes.tts: So, back to the methanogen and E. coli. Their looks hid how far apart they are. A molecule every cell shares revealed it.
scenes.visual: Back to the microscope field: the two grey cells. They recolour, one ORANGE, one BLUE, and slide to opposite ends of the screen, with the tree faint behind them.
scenes.narration: So, back to the methanogen and E. coli. Their looks hid how far apart they are. A molecule every cell shares revealed it.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot holding a white RNA ribbon. Line: 'Read relatedness from a shared molecule, not from looks.'
